stem: A server answers `405` to a `PUT` request on `/profile`. What does the code mean?
options: The client must log in before the request works
The resource exists but does not allow that method
The client has sent too many requests too quickly
The server hit an internal error during the update
explanation: Returning 405 for unused verbs is the recommended REST behavior, and it also blocks HTTP verb tampering.
optionNotes: That is 401.
Correct: Method Not Allowed.
That is 429.
That is 500.

stem: A page at `https://app.example` runs a script that tries to read a response from `https://app.example:8443/data`. What does the same-origin policy decide?
options: Different origin only because the two paths are different
Same origin, because the host name in both URLs is the same
Same origin, because both URLs use the HTTPS scheme
Different origin, because the port differs; CORS must allow the read
explanation: Origin = scheme + host + port. Any difference makes it cross-origin.
optionNotes: Paths are not part of the origin.
Host alone is not enough.
The scheme matches, but the port does not.
Correct: 443 and 8443 are different ports.

stem: What does the `__Host-` prefix on a cookie name guarantee?
options: It is shared automatically with all subdomains of the site
It can be read only by JavaScript running on the same page
It was set with Secure, over HTTPS, with no Domain and Path=/
It is encrypted by the browser before being stored on disk
explanation: OWASP recommends `__Host-` for session cookies so a subdomain cannot overwrite them.
optionNotes: The prefix forbids a Domain attribute, so subdomains do not get it.
Script access is controlled by HttpOnly.
Correct: it is locked to the exact host.
Browsers do not encrypt cookies because of a prefix.

stem: A request carries `Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46UGFzc3cwcmQ=`. What should a tester conclude?
options: The credentials are only Base64-encoded, so TLS is essential
The password has been hashed with SHA-1 by the browser
The header holds a signed JWT issued by the login server
The credentials are encrypted with the server's public key
explanation: Basic authentication sends `user:password` Base64-encoded. Without TLS it is effectively cleartext.
optionNotes: Correct: anyone who sees the header can decode it.
Base64 is not a hash.
A JWT has three dot-separated parts and uses the Bearer scheme.
No key is involved in Base64.

stem: What does PKCE protect in an OAuth 2.0 flow?
options: The authorization code of public clients such as mobile apps
The refresh token that the authorization server stores
The TLS session between the browser and the API server
The signature of the ID token in OpenID Connect flows
explanation: RFC 7636 binds the code to a secret verifier the client created, which a thief who only saw the code does not have.
optionNotes: Correct: a stolen code is useless without the verifier.
PKCE works on the code exchange, not refresh tokens.
TLS protects transport.
ID token signatures are checked separately.

stem: Which statement about hidden form fields is correct from a security point of view?
options: Browsers encrypt them with the session key before they are sent
Users can change them in a proxy, so the server must not trust them
Only administrators can see them when they view the page source
They are removed from the form data when the site uses HTTPS
explanation: Hidden does not mean protected. Validate and authorize on the server.
optionNotes: Browsers send them as plain form data.
Correct (CWE-602).
Anyone can view the page source.
HTTPS protects them in transit, not from the user.

stem: Browsing to `/files/` shows a clickable list of every file in the folder, and error pages print full stack traces. Which OWASP 2025 category fits?
options: A06 Insecure Design
A03 Software Supply Chain Failures
A02 Security Misconfiguration
A07 Authentication Failures
explanation: Use a repeatable hardening baseline, turn off listing, and show generic error pages (CWE-548, CWE-209).
optionNotes: The design may be fine; the deployment is not hardened.
No third-party component is described.
Correct: directory listing and verbose errors are hardening gaps.
Logins are not involved.

stem: A login endpoint receives thousands of attempts, each with a different username and password pair taken from an old breach, from many IP addresses. Which category and control fit?
options: A02 Misconfiguration; turn off directory listing on the site
A05 Injection; parameterized queries on the login endpoint
A08 Integrity Failures; code signing for the login service
A07 Authentication Failures; MFA and breached-password checks
explanation: OWASP's Credential Stuffing cheat sheet adds MFA, device fingerprinting and throttling by account as well as by IP.
optionNotes: Listing is unrelated to logins.
No input is interpreted as code.
Signing does not stop reused passwords.
Correct: this is credential stuffing.

stem: A product review containing script markup is saved, and from then on every customer who opens the product page runs it. Which XSS type is this?
options: Reflected XSS
Stored XSS
DOM-based XSS
Self-XSS
explanation: Encode on output and sanitize rich text with a vetted library; CSP limits the impact.
optionNotes: Reflected XSS needs a crafted request for each victim.
Correct: persistent, served to every visitor.
DOM XSS happens in client-side code.
Self-XSS only affects the person who pastes it.

stem: Why can a CSRF attack change a victim's email address but not read their account page?
options: HTTPS hides every response from all scripts running in the browser
CSRF needs the victim's password before it can read any account page
The same-origin policy stops the attacker's page from reading the response
Servers never return any data in answer to cross-site POST requests
explanation: CSRF is a one-way attack on state-changing actions. XSS is more dangerous because script on the page can read everything.
optionNotes: HTTPS does not decide which scripts can read responses.
CSRF never needs the password.
Correct.
Servers do return data; the attacker simply cannot read it.

stem: An image upload accepts SVG files. The server-side thumbnail tool parses them as XML and one upload makes the server read a local file. Which weakness and fix fit?
options: SSTI; switch to a logic-less template engine
Stored XSS; add a strict Content Security Policy
Path traversal; rename every uploaded file on arrival
XXE; disable DTDs and external entities in the parser
explanation: SOAP bodies, SVG and Office files are all XML. Harden every parser, not just the obvious endpoints.
optionNotes: No template engine is described.
CSP acts in the browser, not in the server-side parser.
Renaming does not stop entity resolution.
Correct: SVG is XML, so the parser is the target.

stem: A cookie decodes to `O:4:"User":2:{s:4:"name";s:3:"bob";s:5:"admin";b:0;}`. What should the tester suspect?
options: The server unserializes a PHP object sent by the client
The cookie is a JWT signed with a weak shared secret
The cookie is a Base64-encoded bcrypt password hash
The cookie holds a cached GraphQL introspection result
explanation: Do not rebuild objects from client data; use JSON with a schema or sign the value and check the signature.
optionNotes: Correct: the `O:` prefix marks a serialized PHP object.
A JWT has three dot-separated Base64url parts.
This is a structured object, not a hash.
Introspection returns JSON.

stem: Web logs show a steady trickle of POST requests to `/images/thumb.php`, a file no page links to, each from an unusual user agent. What should the analyst check first?
options: Whether robots.txt lists the file, which would explain why crawlers call it
Whether the site's images need compressing because of the heavy upload traffic
Whether HSTS is enabled, since the POSTs might be arriving over plain HTTP
Whether it is a web shell: compare with a known-good copy, check spawned processes
explanation: NSA/ASD guidance: file integrity monitoring, known-good comparison and process anomaly detection on web servers.
optionNotes: robots.txt protects nothing.
Image size is irrelevant.
Transport settings do not explain the traffic.
Correct: unlinked scripts receiving POSTs are a classic web shell sign.

stem: Entering an odd expression in a name field returns an error message that names a template engine and a line number. What is the likely class of flaw?
options: Clickjacking of the profile form
Open redirect through the name field
Server-side template injection
Session fixation during sign-up
explanation: Input must be passed to templates as data, never as template code; verbose errors also point to A10.
optionNotes: No framing is involved.
No redirect is involved.
Correct: errors naming the engine are an SSTI indicator.
No session ID is involved.

stem: Which OWASP Top 10 edition does the public CEH v13 course page name, which is why learners should know both lists?
explanation: Map between them: SSRF A10:2021 → A01:2025; Vulnerable Components A06:2021 → A03:2025.
optionNotes: Correct: the course outline predates the 2025 release.
2017 is two editions old.
OWASP's current list is 2025, but the course page names 2021.
2013 is long outdated.

stem: Which tool looks for undocumented request parameters that an endpoint accepts?
options: HTTrack
Arjun
WhatWeb
CeWL
explanation: Hidden parameters (debug flags, role fields) are a frequent source of mass assignment and access-control findings.
optionNotes: HTTrack mirrors a site offline.
Correct.
WhatWeb fingerprints technologies.
CeWL builds wordlists.

stem: Which Burp tool converts data between URL encoding, Base64, HTML entities and hex?
options: Sequencer
Decoder
Intruder
Collaborator
explanation: Decoder is how testers read encoded cookies and parameters, which is why encoding never protects a value.
optionNotes: Sequencer tests token randomness.
Correct.
Intruder sends automated requests.
Collaborator catches out-of-band interactions.

stem: A tester has a list of usernames and a matching list of their default passwords and wants to try row 1 with row 1, row 2 with row 2, and so on. Which Intruder attack type fits?
options: Pitchfork
Cluster bomb
Sniper
Battering ram
explanation: Pitchfork = matched pairs; Cluster bomb = the full cross product.
optionNotes: Correct: parallel lists stepped together.
Cluster bomb tries every combination.
Sniper uses one list.
Battering ram places one value in all positions.

stem: Which tool is built to detect and test OS command injection in web parameters?
options: JoomScan
WPScan
wafw00f
commix
explanation: Defenders see its runs as bursts of shell metacharacters and time-delay probes in one parameter.
optionNotes: JoomScan is for Joomla.
WPScan is for WordPress.
wafw00f detects WAFs.
Correct.

stem: An Nmap run with the `http-enum` script lists `/admin/`, `/phpmyadmin/` and `/backup/` as found. What has the script done?
options: Detected which web application firewall protects the server
Cracked the administrator password for the phpMyAdmin login page
Checked a list of common paths and reported those the server answered
Tested the TLS versions and cipher suites the server accepts
explanation: Remove or protect admin tools and backups; alert on requests for known admin paths.
optionNotes: That is http-waf-detect.
http-enum does not guess passwords.
Correct.
TLS checks use ssl-* scripts.

stem: Which list matches testing categories in the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide?
options: Planning, discovery, attack and reporting, as a generic four-stage penetration test outline
Reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions
Identify, protect, detect, respond and recover, with govern added across all of them in 2024
Information gathering, authentication, authorization, session management, input validation, business logic
explanation: The WSTG is the open reference for how to test each part of a web application.
optionNotes: That is a generic pen test outline, not the WSTG.
That is the Cyber Kill Chain.
Those are NIST CSF functions.
Correct.

stem: A team wants a scheduled scan in its CI pipeline that spiders the staging app and reports passive findings only. Which ZAP option fits?
options: An active scan in ATTACK mode
The ZAP baseline scan
The ZAP fuzzer
A manual Burp Repeater session
explanation: The baseline scan runs the spider for a short time, then passive rules, and returns warnings or failures for CI.
optionNotes: Active scanning sends attacks and takes longer.
Correct.
Fuzzing needs chosen inputs and sends many requests.
Repeater is manual.

stem: An API switched from sequential order IDs to random UUIDs and declared its BOLA problem fixed. Why is that not enough?
options: Random IDs only slow guessing; the server must still check ownership
UUIDs are always encrypted, so nobody can read or reuse them
BOLA only affects GraphQL APIs, not REST APIs with UUIDs
UUIDs in URLs break HTTPS, so the change creates a new flaw
explanation: OWASP lists random IDs as defense in depth only; the real fix is an authorization check per object.
optionNotes: Correct: leaked or shared IDs still work without an ownership check.
UUIDs are identifiers, not encryption.
BOLA affects any API that takes object IDs.
IDs have nothing to do with TLS.

stem: A GraphQL query nests `friends { friends { friends { ... } } }` twenty levels deep and makes the server run out of memory. Which risk and control fit?
options: API9 Improper Inventory Management; retire old versions
API1 BOLA; add object ownership checks
API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption; limit query depth and cost
API10 Unsafe Consumption; validate partner data
explanation: The OWASP GraphQL cheat sheet recommends depth limits, cost analysis, batching limits and timeouts.
optionNotes: No forgotten version is involved.
No other user's object is the issue.
Correct.
No third-party API is involved.

stem: An API returns detailed stack traces, allows every HTTP verb and sends a permissive CORS policy. Which API risk groups these?
options: API8 Security Misconfiguration
API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
API2 Broken Authentication
explanation: Harden every layer: generic errors, method allowlists, strict CORS, TLS and security headers.
optionNotes: Correct.
No business flow is automated.
No property-level issue is described.
Authentication is not described.

stem: Why should a webhook receiver compare signatures with a constant-time function?
options: It removes the need to keep the shared webhook secret on the server
Constant-time functions encrypt the signature before comparing it
It makes the comparison run faster when the server is under load
A normal compare can leak through timing how many characters matched
explanation: GitHub's validation guide uses a constant-time compare such as `hmac.compare_digest` or `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.
optionNotes: The secret is still required.
Comparison does not encrypt anything.
The goal is uniform timing, not speed.
Correct: timing differences can help forge a signature byte by byte.

stem: A receiver parses the webhook JSON, re-serializes it and then computes the HMAC. Valid deliveries keep failing verification. What is the likely cause?
options: HMAC cannot be used with JSON bodies, only with form data
The shared secret must be sent in the webhook URL as well
The HMAC must be computed over the raw body bytes as received
The provider must switch the webhook from HTTPS to HTTP
explanation: Stripe and GitHub both require the raw payload for signature checks.
optionNotes: HMAC works on any bytes.
Secrets must never go in URLs.
Correct: re-serializing changes spacing and key order.
Dropping TLS would make things worse.

stem: How does a webhook differ from polling an API?
options: Webhooks always use SOAP messages, while polling always uses REST calls
The provider pushes events to your URL instead of you asking again and again
Polling is always encrypted with TLS, while webhooks are never encrypted
Webhooks only work inside one private network and never over the internet
explanation: Because anyone can POST to your endpoint, webhook receivers must verify signatures and timestamps.
optionNotes: Both can use any format.
Correct: push versus pull.
Both should use HTTPS.
Webhooks are commonly sent across the internet.

stem: Which ZAP option imports an OpenAPI, SOAP or GraphQL definition and scans the API it describes?
options: Forced browsing
The AJAX Spider
The passive scanner alone
The ZAP API scan
explanation: Scanning from the definition reaches endpoints a crawler would never find, including ones missing from the UI.
optionNotes: Forced browsing guesses paths from a wordlist.
The AJAX Spider crawls browser-rendered pages.
Passive scanning does not import definitions.
Correct.

stem: Which anti-framing control does OWASP now prefer, and why?
options: CSP frame-ancestors, a standard that can list several parents
X-Frame-Options ALLOW-FROM, supported by every modern browser
Frame-busting JavaScript, because attackers cannot disable it
HSTS, because it blocks framing of any page served over HTTP
explanation: X-Frame-Options DENY or SAMEORIGIN is still fine as a legacy fallback.
optionNotes: Correct.
ALLOW-FROM is obsolete and ignored by modern browsers.
Frame-busting scripts can be defeated.
HSTS has nothing to do with framing.

stem: A site sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`. What is the main weakness of this policy?
options: External images are blocked, which breaks most of the site's pages
Inline scripts are allowed, so most injected script tags still run
The page cannot be framed by any site, including its own origin
Session cookies are sent over plain HTTP because of this directive
explanation: Use nonces or hashes instead of `unsafe-inline`, as the OWASP CSP cheat sheet recommends.
optionNotes: This directive only covers scripts.
Correct: `unsafe-inline` undoes most of CSP's XSS protection.
Framing is set by frame-ancestors.
CSP does not control cookie transport.

stem: Which testing approach puts an agent inside the running application to watch code paths while tests run?
options: SCA
SAST
IAST
Threat modeling
explanation: IAST combines some of the code insight of SAST with the runtime view of DAST.
optionNotes: SCA inventories third-party components.
SAST reads code without running it.
Correct: interactive testing.
Threat modeling happens at design time.

stem: Which list gives the five business functions of OWASP SAMM?
options: Plan, Build, Test, Release, Monitor, Improve
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Prepare, Protect, Produce, Respond, Retire
Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations
explanation: SAMM measures and improves the maturity of a software security program.
optionNotes: That is a generic DevOps cycle.
Those are NIST CSF 1.1 functions (CSF 2.0 adds Govern).
That mixes up the SSDF groups, which have no Retire.
Correct.

stem: An attacker types a username containing a line break followed by a fake 'login succeeded for admin' entry, and it appears in the log as its own line. Which control prevents this?
options: Encode or strip line breaks and control characters before logging
Enable HSTS on the login page and the logging endpoint
Rotate the log files every day and compress the old ones
Store the logs on the web server's own local disk only
explanation: The OWASP Logging cheat sheet also asks for central, tamper-resistant log storage.
optionNotes: Correct: this is log injection (CWE-117).
HSTS is a transport control.
Rotation does not stop forged lines.
Storage location does not stop the forgery.

stem: Which control is best suited to detect a new web shell dropped into a website's folder?
options: Output encoding in every template of the application
A longer session timeout for the site's administrators
File integrity monitoring on the web directories
A strict Referrer-Policy header on every page
explanation: Pair it with process monitoring (web server spawning shells) and no execute rights on upload folders.
optionNotes: Encoding prevents XSS, not file drops.
Session length does not reveal new files.
Correct: it alerts on new or changed script files.
Referrer-Policy limits URL leakage.

stem: What do CISA's Secure by Design alerts ask software makers to do about classes such as XSS, OS command injection and directory traversal?
options: Leave these classes to their customers' WAF rules to block
Eliminate whole classes through safe frameworks and APIs
Report them publicly only after they have been exploited
Hide them behind generic error messages in production
explanation: Examples: templating that encodes by default, APIs that never call a shell, path handling that cannot leave a base folder.
optionNotes: CISA puts the burden on the maker, not the customer.
Correct.
The aim is prevention, not disclosure timing.
Hiding errors does not remove flaws.

stem: A tester Base64url-decodes the middle part of a JWT issued by an application and reads the user's email address, role and account number in clear text. What should the report say?
options: The token is broken, since a JWT payload is always encrypted with a key
JWT payloads are only encoded, so they must not carry confidential data
The signature is invalid, since a signed payload cannot be read by anyone
The token has expired, since only expired JWTs can be decoded like this
explanation: A JWT is header.payload.signature in Base64url. Decoding is not a flaw in itself, but it means the payload is public: no secrets or unnecessary personal data belong there, and the server must verify the signature and pin the algorithm.
optionNotes: A signed JWT (JWS) is not encrypted; only a JWE hides its content.
Correct: anyone can decode the payload; the signature only proves it was not changed.
Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality, so a valid token is still readable.
Expiry has nothing to do with whether the payload can be decoded.

stem: A file download filter rejects `../`, yet requests with `%252e%252e%252f` still return files outside the download folder. Which design fix addresses the root cause?
options: Encode every response as HTML entities before sending it to the client
Add `%252e` to the filter's deny list, right next to the plain `../` sequence
Decode input to its canonical form before validating, and avoid raw paths
Move the download feature behind a CAPTCHA to slow automated requests
explanation: Double encoding survives a filter that checks input before it is fully decoded. The fix is to canonicalize, then validate against an allowlist, and never build file paths from raw user input.
optionNotes: Output encoding protects pages against XSS, not file access on the server.
A deny list chases one spelling at a time; the next encoding gets through.
Correct: canonicalize first, then validate; better still, map requests to an allowlist of files.
A CAPTCHA slows automation but leaves the traversal flaw in place.

stem: A password reset flow is coded without bugs, but it lets anyone reset an account by answering security questions such as the user's home town, which staff often post publicly. Which OWASP Top 10:2025 category fits best?
options: A06 Insecure Design: the flaw is in the plan, not the code
A05 Injection: the answers are passed to an interpreter unsafely
A02 Security Misconfiguration: a default setting was left enabled
A04 Cryptographic Failures: the answers are stored without hashing
explanation: Insecure Design covers controls that are missing or weak by design, even when the code is correct. OWASP advises against relying on security questions for resets; a reset token sent to a verified channel is the usual design.
optionNotes: Correct: guessable knowledge-based answers are a design weakness; threat modeling should catch it.
Nothing suggests the answers are interpreted as code or commands.
The weakness is the chosen recovery method, not a leftover default.
Hashing the answers would not help: attackers can still find them.

stem: A user's valid session cookie is captured from traffic on an open Wi-Fi network and replayed from another device, which then acts as that user. Which attack is this, and which controls reduce it?
options: Clickjacking; a frame-ancestors directive in the site's CSP response header
Session fixation; issue a fresh session ID each time the user logs in
Cross-site request forgery; anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies
Session hijacking; HTTPS everywhere, HSTS and the cookie's Secure flag
explanation: Session hijacking reuses a stolen, valid session ID. Serving every page over HTTPS with HSTS and marking the cookie Secure keeps it from travelling in clear text; short lifetimes and re-authentication for sensitive actions limit the damage.
optionNotes: Clickjacking tricks clicks through an invisible frame; it does not steal cookies.
Fixation plants a known ID before login; here an existing ID was stolen.
CSRF makes the victim's own browser send a request; no cookie is stolen.
Correct: stealing and reusing a valid ID is hijacking; encrypting all traffic keeps the cookie off the wire.

stem: Logged in as a customer, a tester changes `/invoices?id=1002` to `id=1003` and receives another customer's invoice. Which OWASP Top 10:2025 category and control fit?
options: A05 Injection; use parameterized queries for the invoice database lookup
A07 Authentication Failures; add multi-factor authentication to logins
A01 Broken Access Control; check ownership of each object on the server
A09 Logging and Alerting Failures; log every invoice that is viewed
explanation: Changing only an object ID and getting someone else's data is IDOR, part of A01 Broken Access Control. The fix is a server-side authorization check on every request; random IDs are only defense in depth.
optionNotes: The ID is a valid value used as intended; nothing is injected.
The tester is properly logged in; the failure is in authorization, not authentication.
Correct: this is an insecure direct object reference; the server must verify the caller owns the record.
Logging helps detect abuse but does not stop access to other customers' data.

stem: A company's code did not change, but its build pulled a new release of an open-source library that had been tampered with in the public package registry. Which OWASP Top 10:2025 category and controls fit?
options: A06 Insecure Design; threat modeling of the company's own internal business flows
A08 Data Integrity Failures; Subresource Integrity on every CDN script tag
A02 Security Misconfiguration; a hardened baseline for the build servers
A03 Software Supply Chain Failures; SBOM, SCA, pinned and verified packages
explanation: A03:2025 grew out of 2021's vulnerable components category and covers the whole chain of dependencies and build tools. Controls include an SBOM, composition analysis, trusted repositories, version pinning and signature checks.
optionNotes: The company's own design is not at fault; a third-party component was altered.
SRI protects scripts loaded in the browser, not packages pulled into a build.
Hardening build servers helps, but the problem is trusting a tampered package.
Correct: tampered or vulnerable dependencies fall under supply chain failures.

stem: A tester has saved two responses to the same request, one made as Alice and one as Bob, and wants the differences highlighted word by word. Which Burp Suite tool fits?
options: Comparer
Sequencer
Collaborator
Intruder
explanation: Burp Comparer highlights the differences between two requests or responses. It is handy in authorization testing, where a small change in a response can show that one user sees another user's data.
optionNotes: Correct: Comparer shows a word-level or byte-level diff of two items.
Sequencer measures how random session tokens are.
Collaborator detects out-of-band interactions from the server.
Intruder sends automated, customized requests.

stem: In an authorized test, one payload list must be placed into all marked positions of a request at the same time, with the same value in each. Which Burp Intruder attack type does this?
options: Sniper
Battering ram
Pitchfork
Cluster bomb
explanation: Intruder's four attack types differ in how payloads fill positions: Sniper (one at a time), Battering ram (same value everywhere), Pitchfork (lists in parallel) and Cluster bomb (every combination).
optionNotes: Sniper uses one list and fills one position at a time.
Correct: battering ram puts the same payload in every position at once.
Pitchfork walks several lists in parallel, one list per position.
Cluster bomb tries every combination of several lists.

stem: During authorization testing, a normal user reaches another normal user's settings page, but no admin function. How is this privilege escalation classified?
options: Horizontal: access to a peer's data at the same privilege level
Vertical: access to the functions of a more privileged role
Session fixation: reuse of an ID planted before login
Forced browsing: guessing paths that are not linked from any page
explanation: Access-control testing separates horizontal escalation (another user's data, same role) from vertical escalation (a higher role's functions). Both are fixed by server-side authorization checks on every request.
optionNotes: Correct: moving sideways to another user with the same role is horizontal escalation.
Vertical escalation means reaching admin or other higher-privilege functions.
Fixation is a session attack, not a type of access-control failure.
Forced browsing finds unlinked content; the question is about whose data is reached.

stem: A team says its webhook endpoint needs no signature check because it only accepts HTTPS. Why is this reasoning wrong?
options: Webhook providers never send over HTTPS, so the endpoint gets plain HTTP
HTTPS certificates expire often, so deliveries fail without a signature
HTTPS protects the channel, but anyone can still POST to the endpoint URL
HTTPS only encrypts the headers, leaving the JSON body readable in transit
explanation: HTTPS encrypts the delivery and authenticates the receiver's server, not the sender. Receivers should compute an HMAC of the raw body with the shared secret, compare it in constant time and check timestamps.
optionNotes: Providers such as GitHub and Stripe deliver over HTTPS.
Certificate renewal is unrelated to proving who sent a delivery.
Correct: TLS does not prove the sender; an HMAC with a shared secret does.
TLS encrypts the whole HTTP message, body included.

stem: A REST endpoint that only handles JSON receives a request whose `Content-Type` is `application/xml`. What does the OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet recommend?
options: Redirect it with 302 to the XML version of the API documentation
Parse it with the XML library and then convert the result to JSON
Answer 200 with an empty body so the client does not learn anything
Reject it with 415 Unsupported Media Type instead of parsing it
explanation: REST services should accept only the content types they expect and answer 415 to anything else. Accepting other formats can bring in parsers the team never meant to expose, such as an XML parser that resolves external entities.
optionNotes: A redirect does not refuse the request and has no security benefit.
Parsing unexpected formats widens the attack surface, for example to XXE.
Pretending success hides errors from legitimate clients and from monitoring.
Correct: validate the content type and refuse unexpected ones with 415.

stem: A team subscribes its webhook to every event type a provider offers, just in case, although it only uses two. Which best practice does this break?
options: Answer each delivery with a 2xx status within the provider's time limit
Subscribe only to the events you need, to limit data sent and load
Store the webhook secret in a vault rather than in the source code
Check the delivery ID so that retried deliveries are processed once
explanation: GitHub's webhook best practices include subscribing to the minimum number of events. Each extra event sends more data to the endpoint and adds load and exposure without any benefit.
optionNotes: Replying quickly is a separate practice; the question is about the subscription.
Correct: fewer events means less data leaving the provider and fewer requests to handle.
Secret storage matters, but it is not what this setup gets wrong.
Duplicate handling is a separate practice about retries.

stem: Behind the OWASP Core Rule Set, a request matches three rules that each add a few points, and it is blocked although no single rule would block it alone. Why?
options: Detection-only mode turns a match on three rules into a blocking rule
The paranoia level blocks any request that matches more than one rule
Anomaly scoring adds up rule points and blocks above a set threshold
The positive security model blocks all requests matching several rules
explanation: The Core Rule Set uses anomaly scoring: each matching rule adds points, and a blocking decision is made when the request's total reaches the inbound threshold. This reduces false positives from single weak matches.
optionNotes: Detection-only mode logs and never blocks.
Paranoia levels decide which rules run, not how many matches are allowed.
Correct: CRS rules add to an anomaly score, and the request is blocked once the total passes the threshold.
CRS is mainly a negative model built on attack signatures, scored as anomalies.

stem: A site sends a correct HSTS header, yet a user's very first visit, typed as `http://`, can still be downgraded on hostile Wi-Fi. Which addition closes that gap?
options: Setting a much longer max-age value in the HSTS header field
Getting the domain onto the browsers' HSTS preload list
Adding X-Frame-Options: DENY to every HTTPS response
Serving a 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS on every page
explanation: HSTS works only after the browser has received the header over HTTPS. Preloading puts the domain in a list built into browsers, so even the first request goes over HTTPS; it needs includeSubDomains and the preload directive.
optionNotes: max-age only matters after the browser has seen the header once.
Correct: browsers ship with the preload list, so they use HTTPS even on the first visit.
X-Frame-Options stops framing; it does not force HTTPS.
The HTTP request before the redirect is exactly what can be intercepted.

stem: A support assistant built on a language model summarizes incoming customer e-mails. One e-mail contains hidden text telling the model to include other customers' tickets in its summary, and it does. Which OWASP LLM risk and control fit?
options: Prompt injection; treat content as untrusted and limit the model's data access
Improper output handling; encode all of the model's output before showing it in HTML
Data and model poisoning; retrain the model on a curated, reviewed data set
Unbounded consumption; cap the number of tokens each request may consume
explanation: Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in content the model processes. Defenses include treating all external content as untrusted, separating instructions from data, and giving the model access only to the data the current user may see.
optionNotes: Correct: instructions hidden in processed content override the app's intent; least privilege limits what they can reach.
Output handling is about rendering model output unsafely; here the model followed injected instructions.
Nothing suggests the training data was changed; the instruction arrived in an e-mail.
Nothing here exhausts resources; the model leaked data it should not reach.
